A black stone is found in the Nile similar to a bean; when it is seen, dogs do not bark. You shall carry a dog’s tongue underneath your shoe against your toe, or if you carry a dried dog’s heart with you, according to Sextus. Carry hare’s hair or dung, according to Pliny. Or, carry the severed tail of a young weasel on your foot, or give a frog to it in a morsel of food; all these are for avoiding the barking of dogs. Nigidius says that dogs flee the sight of one who has expelled a tick from a dog and carried it for a little while. Oppian:

> *But if you carry a small piece of a hyena’s skin*
> *that has been cut off, at once the whelps and fierce dogs*
> *will be struck with sharp terror, and they will not bark*
> *at you as you pass, even if they had barked before.*

### *How a dog may not be able to run.*

If you smear the wings <note>referring to the dog's legs or joints as "wings" in a metaphorical or archaic anatomical sense</note> with oil, for it will be hindered in its running; this will happen in this way.

### *How a hawk may be spirited.*

You will animate a bird against its prey, so that it might attack large birds; steep the bait, which it uses at the time of hunting, in wine, or if it is a goshawk, give it a little vinegar. When you wish for it to fly, give it three morsels of meat steeped in wine, or pour wine into a dove chick's beak, then make it fly. Thus:

### *You will make partridges more pugnacious,*

If you give them sprigs of maidenhair fern <note>original: "adianti"</note> in their food, according to Pliny, and:

### *Roosters become more pugnacious,*

By giving them garlic in their food when they are about to fight; from which, in an old comedy, those who are <term>eskorodismenoi</term> <gloss>garlic-stuffed; original: "ἐσκοροδισμένοι"</gloss>, that is, fed on garlic, are spoken of in a very witty way as being vehement and overly inclined to battle.

### *That a bird may not fly high,*

Pull out the tail feathers that direct the course upwards, and thus it will fly in a circle below. If you wish:

### *That a bird may not be able to fly,*

Cut the upper and lower tendons of the wing, and it remains without harm; the bird will not fly, and in this way they do not escape in aviaries.

<summary>This page lists folkloric and practical methods for managing animals in the context of hunting and bird-catching, including remedies to stop dogs from barking and techniques to influence the vigor or flight capability of hawks and game birds.</summary>
<keywords>bird-catching, dog behavior, hunting lore, Oppian, Pliny, animal performance, hawk training, poultry management</keywords>

The sun itself, indeed, illuminates the other stars not so much by the magnitude of its divinity as by its holiness. Believe this, O Asclepius, to be the second god who governs all things and illuminates all living beings in the world, whether they are animate or inanimate. 

For if the world is a living creature, always having been, being, and destined to be, then nothing in the world is mortal. For in each living part that exists within the world, just as in one and the same living creature that is always alive, there is no place for mortality. Therefore, God himself must be most full of life and eternity, if it is necessary for him always to live. The sun, therefore, is like the world, eternal; and thus it is the constant governor of vital things, or rather the frequent provider and dispenser of all their vitality. Therefore, God is the eternal governor of the living or vital things that are in the world, and the eternal dispenser of life itself. He has dispensed it once by an eternal law, providing life to all vital beings in the manner that I shall describe.

<summary>This passage defines the sun as a secondary deity that acts as an eternal governor and dispenser of life to all beings within the living world, emphasizing the world's inherent immortality.</summary>
<keywords>Asclepius, Hermes Trismegistus, The Sun, Divine Governor, Life, Eternity, Living World, Vitality</keywords>

And there are things more marvelous than these: for on the Attic shore, the sea sounds like a cithara <note>a stringed instrument similar to a lyre or zither</note>. A certain rock at Megara produces musical notes when struck, so great is the power of Music. It itself soothes the soul, elevates the mind, incites soldiers to war, and alleviates the labors and weariness of individual tasks. It recalls the fallen and the desperate, and comforts travelers. The Arabs say that camels carrying burdens are comforted by their singing guides. In a similar way, those carrying heavy loads sing, and are enabled and lightened by it: for song produces pleasure and readiness. It mitigates the angry, makes the sad and anxious joyful, pacifies the discordant, and tempers the madness of the deranged; it dissipates vain thoughts. Hence it is that Democritus and Theophrastus affirm that certain diseases of the body and mind can be cured or induced in this way. Thus we read that Terpander and Arion the Methymnaean <note>These were famous semi-legendary Greek musicians known for their command over the natural world through music.</note>

<summary>This page continues a discussion on the effects of music, describing its power to soothe the mind, ease labor, and influence physical health, citing the observations of Varro, Democritus, and Theophrastus.</summary>

For the good is innate to truth, together with life and light, and no avenger came to pass beyond it. Truly, all the avengers were cast back by a certain sudden impulse. You have understood, my son, the mode of rebirth itself; the intellectual generation is composed by the presence of the number ten, which rejects the number twelve. And we have contemplated this from the generation itself. Whoever, therefore, because of the kindness of the generation that is according to God, loses his bodily sense, knows himself to be composed of divine things and, having become unswerving, rejoices in the divine power with his whole mind. **TATIVS.** O father, I conceive this not by the intuition of the eyes, but by the act of the mind, which is exercised through inner strengths. I am in heaven, in earth, in water, in air. I am in animals, in trees, in the body, before the body, and after the body. But I would have you tell me this further: how are the avenging shadows repelled by the ten powers from the number twelve? What is the mode, Trismegistus? **TRIS.** This tabernacle, O son, is constituted from the zodiacal circle, which consists of that number twelve. And the numbers are eleven, and one which is omniform according to the ideas of nature, for the wandering and circuit of man. Therefore, those avengers are in a way separated from one another, yet in acting they are in a way joined, as, for example, recklessness is inseparable from wrath. Rightly, therefore, according to right reason, there is an interval as far as the ten powers, that is, they are repelled by the number ten. The number ten, O son, is the generator of the soul. But life...

<summary>Hermes explains how the intellectual generation of the divine soul, governed by the number ten, rejects and repels the twelve vices associated with the zodiac and the material body.</summary>
<keywords>Hermes Trismegistus, Tatius, rebirth, number ten, number twelve, zodiac, intellectual generation, avengers, powers</keywords>

There are, therefore, gods who are the princes of all species; these are followed by gods of whom the prince is <term>ousia</term> <gloss>essence/being</gloss>. These sensible ones are of both origins and are similar to them, they who through sensible nature construct all things, one through the other, each illuminating its own work. Of the heavens, or whatever is comprehended under that name, the <term>ousiarches</term> <gloss>prince of essence</gloss> is Jupiter. For through the heavens, Jupiter offers life to all. The <term>ousiarches</term> of the sun is <term>lumen</term> <gloss>light</gloss>. For the good of light is infused into us through the orb of the sun. Of the thirty-six stars (whose name is Horoscopii) always fixed in the same place, their <term>ousiarches</term> or prince is he whom they call <term>Pantomorphon</term> <gloss>all-formed</gloss> or Omniform. He who, through diverse species, makes diverse forms. The seven spheres which are called erratic have their <term>ousiarchas</term>, that is, their princes, which they call Fate, <term>heimarmene</term> <gloss>destiny</gloss>, by which all things are changed, with the firmest stability of the law of nature, and varied by sempiternal agitation. Truly, the air is the instrument, or machine of all things, through which all things are done. But the <term>ousiarches</term> of this is secondary. To mortals, mortal things; and to these, similar things. Since these things are so, moving from the lowest to the highest, all things pertaining to themselves are naturally connected, so that to mortals, mortal things, and to sensible things, sensible things are annexed. Truly, the sum of governance obeys that highest Lord, so that they are not many, or rather, they are one. For all things hanging from one, and flowing down rather from him, when they are at a distance, are believed to be very many and divided. But when united, they are one, or rather two, from whence all things are made and by whom they are made: that is, from the matter of which they are made, and from his will, by whose nod other things are effected. ASCLE. This is again the argument which is, O Trismegistus. TRISME. Such it is, O Asclepius. For God, whether as father, or lord—

For indeed, arsenic certainly cannot be fixed in the least, unless the operating artist has an equal knowledge of its tingeing spirit, regarding which all philosophers have slumbered, attempting in vain to accomplish anything from it. Therefore, whoever is ignorant of this spirit should have no hope of fixing it, nor of attributing to it the virtue by which it might acquire the perfection of transmutation. For this reason, I make it known to all that the whitening about which mention has been made is drawn from a false foundation, and that by it copper is falsely whitened, not transmuted. Sophists mixed Venus <note>alchemical term for copper</note> masked and painted in this manner with a double portion of Luna <note>alchemical term for silver</note> and sold it to goldsmiths and coiners: but finally, they transformed themselves into false coiners, not only those who sold, but also those who bought. Some of the sophists took red arsenic instead of white, and this itself departed into a false art. For in whatever way it may be prepared, it exhibits nothing but whiteness. Some have proceeded further, to common sulfur, which they cooked in this way with vinegar, lye, or very sharp urines, day and night, until it emerged white. Afterward, they elevated it from common salt and eggshell <note>calcium carbonate, often used in sublimation processes</note>, cooked and sublimated it through sublimation, and that many times; nevertheless, it always remained combustible, even though white: yet by this, to fix the crude mercury...

<summary>The author warns against fraudulent alchemical methods, specifically the ineffective use of arsenic and common sulfur to whiten copper, labeling these practitioners as "sophists" or counterfeiters who fail to achieve true transmutation.</summary>
<keywords>arsenic, sulfur, Sophists, whitening, Venus, copper, Luna, silver, transmutation, fixation</keywords>

where they should have taken <term>pyrite</term>, they took <term>sulphur</term>, <term>salt</term>, <term>metal</term>, and various other materials, in which there is no operation; and although these things are expensive in shops, they are of no value at all in the work. Our matter, however, is not bought from any shop, yet it is found there every day, and merchants throw it into the streets. It is enough, therefore, that it is found for free: but the matter of our <term>stone</term> is compared to all those things with which the workers labor. For our stone is our <term>salt</term>, our <term>Mercury</term>, <term>verdigris</term>, <term>niter</term>, <term>sal ammoniac</term>, <term>Mars</term> <gloss>iron</gloss>, <term>sulphur</term>, and countless others of this kind, yet not dug from wild and open mountains with hammers and other instruments. Our stone is extracted solely from our own mountains and fountains: our <term>salt</term> is found in our <term>salt-spring</term>; our <term>metal</term>, <term>Mercury</term>, and <term>sulphur</term> are produced from our earth, and not from wild, foreign, and open mountains. All of this, the practitioners do not understand, nor can they believe or grasp it. For the Lord has darkened and closed their senses, for which reason they have used these things otherwise than was required and have not aimed at the mark at all. Nevertheless, they have persisted in this contrary direction and followed their own stubborn heads; for instance, when they should have distilled gently, they <term>sublimed</term> with a strong fire, scorched the <term>aqua fortis</term> <gloss>strong water/nitric acid</gloss>, and burned the nature of the operation and the substances themselves instantly, reducing them to nothing. When they also should have <term>dissolved</term>, they <term>coagulated</term> there instead, and again, like those unskilled in things, they handled the matter unskillfully. They fell into doubt and maintained with lying words that the art was not true but false, in which, however, they are justly lying: for their own ignorance has shamefully deceived them, which must be attributed to their own dark and murky cunning, since, according to their obscure intellect, they interpreted words otherwise than they sounded. For example, when the Philosophers spoke of <term>calcining</term> (which they call grinding), those unskilled <term>Philosophasters</term> <gloss>would-be philosophers</gloss> understood it as burning and reduced the things entirely to ashes, so that nothing could be made from them. Likewise, when the Philosophers <term>dissolve</term> or transmute into water, those <term>wiseacres</term> burned the nature with <term>aqua fortis</term>, and with that same water, which has no power in...

<summary>The author critiques pseudo-alchemists who misunderstand the nature of materials and operations by using store-bought substances and excessive heat, leading to failure and disbelief in the Art.</summary>
<keywords>pyrite, sulphur, salt, Mercury, calcining, dissolving, subliming, Philosophasters, aqua fortis, ignorance of the Art</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>the fire requires temperance, and the succession of that increase must be gradual, with caution, until it is fixed in its lime <gloss>powdered oxide</gloss>, so that it does not easily return into a body, in order that a greater fire may be applied to it for the perfection of its lime. Likewise, lest it happen that one errs in <term>Jupiter</term> <gloss>tin</gloss>, because of the difficulty of its reduction <gloss>conversion back to metal</gloss>, such that if he places its lime into reduction, it happens to him that it does not reduce, but he finds it in its previous state or converted into glass, and judges its reduction to be impossible. We say indeed that if he does not apply a great fire in the reduction of <term>Jupiter</term>, it will not reduce. If, however, he applies a great one, it is not necessarily the case that it will reduce, but it is possible that it will reduce into vitrification <gloss>turning to glass</gloss>. And that is because <term>Jupiter</term> has a fugitive substance of <term>argentum vivum</term> <gloss>quicksilver/mercury</gloss> enclosed in the depths of its nature. If it draws out a long stay in the fire, it will flee and leave the body deprived of humidity, so that it is found to be more suited to vitrification than to the fusion <gloss>melting</gloss> of a metallic body. For everything deprived of its own humidity gives no fusion except a vitrifying one. And therefore, it is necessarily required that one hastens to reduce it quickly with an extremely swift application of fire. Otherwise, it will not be reduced. Therefore, he will practice at this, and he will know.

The second method of calcination of these two bodies, <term>Saturn</term> <gloss>lead</gloss> and <term>Jupiter</term> <gloss>tin</gloss>, which is perfected by the acuteness of salt, is that a quantity of salt be thrown over the face of them, quantity after quantity, very often during their fusion, and mixed with much agitation by an iron rod, over the fire, until they are turned into ash through the mixture of salt. And afterward, the lime of them is to be perfected through the same method of perfection, with its considerations. But in this, there is also a difference in the calcination of these two bodies. Because <term>plumbum</term> <gloss>lead</gloss> is converted into powder more easily than <term>Jupiter</term> <gloss>tin</gloss> from the first labors of calcination, yet its lime is not perfected more easily than that of <term>Jupiter</term>. The cause of this depends on the fact that <term>Saturn</term> <gloss>lead</gloss> has a more fixed humidity than <term>Jupiter</term> <gloss>tin</gloss>.

<summary>This page details the risks of overheating tin and lead during reduction, warning against vitrification, and describes an alternative method of calcination using salt as an agent.</summary>
<keywords>Jupiter, Saturn, calcination, reduction, vitrification, quicksilver, humidity, salt</keywords>

829. Since religion resides in the highest parts of a person, and from these highest parts his lower parts live and shine, and because Mohammed occupies their minds along with their religion, therefore some Mohammed is always placed in their view. And so that they may turn their faces to the East, upon which is the Lord, he is placed below the Christian center. It is not Mohammed himself who wrote the <term>Alcoranus</term> <gloss>Koran</gloss>, but another who performs his duty; nor is it always the same one, but he is changed. Once it was a man from Saxony, who, having been captured by the Algerians, became a Mohammedan. Because he had also been a Christian, he was prompted several times to speak with them about the Lord, that He was not the Son of Joseph, but the Son of God Himself. To this Mohammed, others succeeded later. In the place where that representative Mohammed has his seat, a fire appears like a torch, so that he may be known; but that fire is not visible to others than Mohammedans.

830. Mohammed himself, who wrote the Koran, does not come into view today. It was told to me that in the earliest times he presided over them, but because he wished to rule over all things of their religion as God, he was ejected from his seat, which he had held under the Catholics, and was sent down to the right side near the south. Once, a certain society of Mohammedans was stirred up by malicious spirits to acknowledge Mohammed as God. In order that the sedition might be quieted, Mohammed was brought up from the lower earth and shown, and then he also was seen by me. He appeared like those corporeal spirits who have no interior perception, his face inclining toward black, and I heard him speaking these words: *I am your Mohammed*; and immediately he seemed as if subsiding.

831. Mohammedans are hostile to Christians primarily because of the faith of three Divine Persons, and thence the worship of three Gods, as many Creators; and furthermore to the Roman Catholics because of their genuflections before images, and hence they call the latter idolaters and the former fanatics, saying that they make a three-headed God, and that they say "one" but mutter "three," and therefore that they divide Omnipotence and from one and of one make three. They say that they are like fauns with three horns, one for each God, and together three for one, and that they pray thus, sing thus, and sound forth from their pulpits thus.

832. Mohammedans have, like all nations that acknowledge one God and love what is just and do what is good from religion, their own Heaven, but it is outside the Christian one. However, the Mohammedan Heaven is divided into two parts. In the lower one they live honestly with several wives, but from there no others are raised into the higher Heaven except those who renounce concubines and acknowledge the Lord our Savior, and at the same time His dominion over Heaven and Hell. I heard that it is impossible for them to think that God the Father and our Lord are one, but that it is possible for them to believe that He rules over the Heavens and Hells because He is the Son of the God the Father. This faith among them is that through which ascent into the higher Heaven is granted to them by the Lord.

833. That the Mohammedan religion has been received by more kingdoms than the Christian religion can be a scandal to those who think about Divine Providence and at the same time believe that no one can be saved unless they are born a Christian. But the Mohammedan religion is not a scandal to those who believe that all things are of Divine Providence; these inquire in what it consists, and they also find it. It consists in this, that the Mohammedan religion acknowledges the Lord as the Greatest Prophet, the Wisest of all, and also as the Son of God. But because they have made only the Koran the book of their religion, and hence Mohammed, who wrote it, has settled into their thoughts, and they follow him with some worship, therefore they think little about our Lord. That it may be fully known that that religion was raised up by the Divine Providence of the Lord for the sake of destroying the idolatries of many nations, it will be told in some order, but first concerning the origin of idolatries. Before that religion there was idolatrous worship.

CLXXXVI.
ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,

### On the images of the head and tail of the Moon's dragon. Chap. XLV.

<note>A woodcut depicts a serpent or dragon coiled into a circular shape resembling the Greek letter Theta (Θ). The creature has the head of a bird (a hawk) and a pointed tail. Within the circular body, there is a central vertical line crossed by a shorter horizontal line, with small astrological or symbolic marks at the terminals.</note>

They also used to make an image of the head and tail of the Moon's dragon <note>the lunar nodes, where the Moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic</note>, namely, the figure of a serpent between an airy and a fiery circle, with the head of a hawk surrounding them, in the likeness of the Greek letter theta. They made it when Jupiter occupied the mid-heaven with the head <note>of the dragon</note>; they affirm that this image contributes much to the success of petitions. They wished by this image to denote a good and fortunate spirit <note>original: "dęmonem"—in this context, a tutelary spirit or genius</note>, and they wished to figure it through the image of a serpent: for the Egyptians and the Phoenicians celebrate this as a divine animal above all others, and they celebrate its divine nature, because in it, more than in other animals, exists a sharper and more ample spirit. This is shown both by its swift movement without any feet, hands, or other instruments, and because it renews its age from time to time and becomes young again. They made a similar image of the tail when the Moon was eclipsed in the tail, or was badly affected by Saturn or Mars, and they made it to induce anxiety and infirmity, and they called it an evil spirit. A certain Hebrew once enclosed such an image in a double golden belt, which Blanca, daughter of the Duke of Bourbon, gave as a gift to her husband, Peter, the first king of Spain of that name (whether knowingly or unknowingly). When he was girded with it, he seemed to himself to be surrounded by a serpent; having later discovered that a magic power was inserted into the belt, he repudiated his wife for that reason.

### On the images of the Mansions of the Moon. Chap. XLVI.

They also made images in the individual mansions of the Moon. In the first, for the destruction of someone, they made in an iron ring an image of a black man wearing a hair shirt and girded, throwing a lance with his right hand; they sealed this in black wax and fumigated it with liquid storax and uttered imprecations. In the second, against the anger of a prince and for reconciliation with him, they sealed in white wax and mastic the image of a crowned king, and they fumigated it with aloe wood. In the third, they made an image in a silver ring, the measure of which was square and the figure of which was a woman well dressed, sitting on a chair, with her right hand raised over her head; they sealed and fumigated it with musk, camphor, and aromatic nail <note>likely clove</note>. They asserted that this bestows prosperity of fortune and every good thing. In the fourth, for vengeance and separation, enmity, and malevolence, they sealed in red wax the image of a soldier sitting on a horse, holding a serpent in his right hand, and they fumigated it with red myrrh and storax. In the fifth, for the favor of kings and officials and a good reception, they sealed from silver the head of a man, and they fumigated it with sandalwood. In the sixth, to place love between two, they sealed in white wax two images embracing each other, and they fumigated it with aloe wood and amber. You are now approaching the end of your work, and have almost completed your task. But while pretending to worship God, they do not perform the only things by which God is worshipped. For God, as the Father of all, needs nothing; but it is good for us when we worship Him through justice, chastity, and other virtues, making our very life a process toward Him through imitation and instruction from Him. For instruction purges the mind, while imitation deifies the affection by acting toward Him. He spoke truly when he preached God as Father and said with what customs He must be worshipped. The prophetic books of the Hebrews are full of these precepts, when the life of the holy is either praised or blamed. But who said this to him, or inspired him, if not the diabolical spirit, such a vain and apt lie, that Christians should revere rather than hate the demons whom the Hebrews were forbidden to worship? But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshipped, and the celestial holy angels and the virtues of God, whom we venerate and love as most blessed citizens in this our mortal pilgrimage, forbids sacrifice in the law that He gave to His people, the Hebrews; and He spoke very threateningly, saying: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out." And lest anyone think that it was a command not to sacrifice to the very evil and earthly spirits—whom this man calls mimes or lesser ones—because they also were called "gods" in the holy scriptures, not by the Hebrews

<column-break/>

but by the Gentiles: which the seventy interpreters clearly set down in the Psalm, saying, "For all the gods of the Gentiles are demons." Lest, therefore, anyone should think that it was forbidden to sacrifice to these demons, but permitted to sacrifice to celestial ones, either to all or to some, he immediately added: "unless to the Lord alone," that is, "unless to the Lord only," lest perhaps one who says "to the Lord alone" might think that there is only one God to whom one must sacrifice. That this is not to be understood in that way is very easily found in the Greek scriptures. Therefore, the God of the Hebrews—to whom even this philosopher gives such great testimony—gave the law to His Hebrew people, written in the Hebrew language, not obscure and unknown, but now spread among all nations, in which law it is written: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, unless to the Lord only." What is the need in this, His law and His prophets, to seek much concerning this matter? Rather, there is no need to seek; for they are not obscured or erased, but clear and frequent, and I shall collect them and place them in this my disputation, by which it appears clearer than light that the true and supreme God wished to be sacrificed to by no one at all except to Himself alone. Behold, this one thing, briefly or rather weightily, threateningly, but truthfully said by that God whom their most learned men preach: let it be heard, feared, fulfilled, lest eradication follow the disobedient. "He who sacrifices to gods," He says, "shall be rooted out, unless to the Lord only." Not because He is in need of anything, but because it is expedient for us that we should be His. For it is sung to Him in the sacred letters of the Hebrews: "I said to the Lord, You are my God, for You do not need my goods." But the most excellent and best sacrifice of this God is we ourselves. This is His city, the mystery of which we celebrate with our offerings, which are known to the faithful, just as I have disputed in the preceding books. For the oracles of the Hebrew prophets interpreted that the victims which the Jews offered in the shadow of the future would cease, and that the nations would offer one sacrifice from the rising of the sun even to its setting, just as we now see being done.

The matter in which <term>YHWH</term> <gloss>the Tetragrammaton</gloss> <term>Elohim</term> <gloss>God</gloss> is recognized is that they are enacted in all the attributes that conclude in the attribute of Justice and the attribute of Mercy. As you will find in the creation of the first man, in his judgment, in his expulsion, and in all those matters, you will find that they all came about through the attribute of Justice and the attribute of Mercy, and everything was in complete perfection—in mercy and justice, everything according to what is appropriate in true judgment. According to this principle, the Torah says, "The Rock, His work is perfect" <note>Deuteronomy 32:4</note>. The explanation of the verse is as follows: The Rock, who decrees the judgment with force, does not act in cruelty. He does not decree the judgment except that "His work is perfect." Rather, the judgment that He decreed previously, He consulted regarding it with the two attributes, Grace <note>Chesed</note> and Justice <note>Din</note>. This is "His work is perfect," for the language of "perfect" <note>Hebrew: *tamim*</note> is the secret of two things. It is as if it said "twins" <note>Hebrew: *te'omim*</note>, but in honorable language, he used the word "perfect" for the two things above, and below he used the word "twins." Thus it says, "And they shall be twins" <note>Exodus 26:24</note>. Below, they shall be "perfect" at the top <note>referring to the construction of the Tabernacle's corner boards</note>. Below, there are twins; above, they are perfect, because below they appear as two things, a thing and its opposite, as one assisting and one accusing. But above, everything is one intention. Whether it is the assistant or the accuser, both have one intention, and there is no hatred or love there, and no favoritism, but true judgment. Therefore, it says "His work is perfect," for He consulted in justice and in mercy and decreed the judgment, and this is the secret of true judgment. And what it says, "For all His ways are justice" <note>Deuteronomy 32:4</note>, means everything is for the eye of every observer, as it says, "For all His ways are justice." You already know that the judgment is included in justice and in mercy, for the judgment is opposite Jacob, who is the middle line <note>Tiferet</note>, who is the mediator between two tents, which are Abraham and Isaac. Abraham is opposite Grace, Isaac is opposite Justice, and Jacob decides between them, "a plain man, dwelling in tents" <note>Genesis 25:27</note>. And the judgment is opposite Jacob, drawing from Grace on the side of Abraham and from Justice on the side of Isaac. Thus it says, "Justice and righteousness in Jacob You have performed" <note>Psalm 99:4</note>. And the prophet said, "Correct me, YHWH, but with justice; not in Your anger, lest You diminish me" <note>Jeremiah 10:24</note>. The explanation of the verse is: "Correct me, YHWH, but with justice"—what he said "but" <note>Hebrew: *akh*</note> serves to divide, meaning in half of the attribute of Justice, which is Grace, for the judgment is half justice and half grace. Therefore he said "but with justice," and he said after that, "not in Your anger, lest You diminish me," and he revealed the secret of diminishing the half of the justice from the side of the anger. Therefore, the judgment depends on Jacob, who is the patriarch of the tribes. He knew the great suffering of the children, and when the Holy One, blessed be He, decrees concerning them, He seeks for them mercy and righteousness. The secret is "And YHWH of Hosts shall be exalted in judgment" <note>Isaiah 5:16</note>. What is written after it? "And the Holy God is sanctified in righteousness." This means that when the judgment is raised from the rest of the justice, and it clears a path to the attribute of God, which is the secret of what is said, "And the Holy God is sanctified in righteousness," it means when YHWH of Hosts is exalted in judgment, the attribute of God comes, which is above, and it performs righteousness, and the judgment works. This is the secret of what they said, that the judgment is included in grace and justice, and it says "Justice and righteousness in Jacob You have performed." The great secret is "Righteousness and justice are the foundation of Your throne" <note>Psalm 89:15</note>, for righteousness is sometimes justice according to its reception in abundance, as I have explained, for righteousness is great justice in strength. But when judgment participates with it, then the throne is established in mercy. And if He is exalted in judgment and reaches until the Grace and the Truth, together they are called the "Shining Countenances," then everything becomes great mercy, and this is the secret of "They shall go before..."

### **Torah** is light. These commandments mentioned in this portion are divided into three parts, which are the three pillars upon which the world stands: Torah, <term>Avodah</term> <gloss>Service/Worship</gloss>, and acts of kindness. Torah is the commandment "You shall not add nor diminish," which points to the perfection of the Torah. This is as the philosophers said: a thing that is perfect in total perfection cannot be called lacking or excessive. For if it were lacking, it would not be perfect; and if it could accept an addition, it would be found not to have been perfect. Therefore, the definition of the perfect is that which has neither lack nor excess. It is known that the Torah depends on His great Name, which is <term>Yod-Heh-Vav-Heh</term>, "The Torah of the Lord is perfect," as I have elaborated on this in my <term>Masechet Shevuot</term> <gloss>Tractate of Oaths</gloss>, chapter "Torah is Light." And as it is written in the <term>Zohar</term> regarding this verse: "This is My Name and this is My memorial." <term>Yod-Heh</term> with "My Name" equals 365, and <term>Vav-Heh</term> with "My memorial" equals 248. It is written, "I am the first and I am the last." This is the absolute perfection, having in it no deficiency nor addition. Concerning this comes the warning, "You shall not do so unto the Lord your God." This is a warning against erasing the Name or tearing a stone from the Temple. The letters of the Name are in the house where He, blessed be He, dwells, and so too is the Temple. It is written, "I am the Lord, My Name..." The letters are like a closure for the house, and His Name, blessed be He, is the soul for them. One who destroys His house, so to speak, destroys Him. This is the secret of "You shall not do so unto the Lord your God." <term>Avodah</term> is the majority of the commandments mentioned in this portion. The commandment came to have a fixed place, coming into the Chosen House, and he spoke a word with reason: "To His habitation shall you seek and you shall come there." "To His habitation" hints at the <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss>, which is the palace of the Name <term>Yod-Heh-Vav</term>, as it is written, "He shall dwell in the tent of His holiness." As it is said, "Do not fear, for it shall dwell with Me," for in the Temple, the glory is unified in the splendor of His people. This is "to His name, His name there," as the <term>Targum</term> <gloss>Aramaic translation</gloss> says: "to cause His <term>Shekhinah</term> to dwell." Around the place of holiness, the wicked walk, for they are the <term>Qlippah</term> <gloss>husk/shell of impurity</gloss>; therefore, "Take heed to yourself lest you offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see."

### **And sometimes** sparks of holiness spread outward, and it is a commandment to return them, to bring them inward. This is the secret of the commandment to eat the firstborns and the sacrifices outside the city of the Chosen House. Then the branch returns to its root, and it is written of them, "There you shall bring up," meaning there they shall have an elevation, and not outside. Since the Chosen House, which is in the Holy Land, is where holiness resides, we were commanded to be "turn from evil" by destroying all the places where the nations worshipped. One must uproot and eradicate after them, and this is commanded specifically in the Holy Land. Its secret alludes to the ten nations whose power is not <term>avodah zarah</term> <gloss>idol worship</gloss> per se, but the matter is that the nations who are in the Land of Israel, under the rule of the honored Name, worship the Name by "cutting the shoots" <note>A talmudic metaphor for heresy</note>, and this is true idolatry. However, in the lands outside the Land of Israel, they are under the rule of external forces. Just as there is a great prohibition to tear one stone from the holiness, so, on the contrary, it is a great commandment to destroy and eradicate an "apostate city" <note>A city whose inhabitants have been led into idolatry</note> and not to rebuild it, for its place is defiled. Likewise, the inciter and the one who leads astray must be uprooted and eradicated, for he is from the defilement of the primordial serpent that incited; and the Holy One, blessed be He, immediately said, "Cursed is the serpent," therefore there is no reviving the powers of the inciter. The command came not to love him and not to listen to him, as is stated regarding the serpent, "I will put enmity between you and the woman." Also, a false prophet is like an inciter. Let us return to the matter: the root of holiness is the Chosen House and Jerusalem. This is the reason for the first fruits, that the priests have no permission to eat them until they are placed in the Chosen House, for the first fruits, which are the beginning, indicate great holiness, as I have written elsewhere. Therefore, to a holy place they shall go, and from there they shall take their wisdom, for they are holy to God, and they shall eat in Jerusalem. This is the secret of the "lesser holy things" and the "second tithe," that their consumption is in Jerusalem. This is the grain, and the wine, and the oil, which are the fathers of fathers of all sustenance. It is forbidden to eat the lesser holy things until after the blood is tossed, for the blood is the soul. After that is the permission to indulge and derive benefit. Know that just as the <term>Avodah</term>, which is the sacrifice, is a sacrifice to the Lord, so it is with the worker <note>The one performing the service</note>, for the essence of the work is that he offers himself, in the secret of "When a man offers from among you." The burnt offering is entirely consumed, for it comes because of the thoughts of the heart, which is spiritual, and he confesses all night... the serpent does not hinder him. And the lesser holy things are the perfection of the soul and the body.

### **The secret** of the firstborn is the secret of Israel, who are called holy, as it is written, "Israel is My firstborn." He has compassion on them, "You shall guard them," and they are called "the flock of My pasture." Therefore, it is eaten only by the priests. The secret of eating the holy things corresponds to their blemishes and cracks, for Israel is holy, and Israel is called "Man." And it was holy, but afterward, a blemish fell upon it after it sinned and was clothed in "garments of skin." But it has a redemption, in the secret of "I will give man in your stead." This was the secret of <term>Azazel</term> <gloss>a desolate place for the scapegoat</gloss>, and he shall bear their iniquities. As it is said, their iniquities are those that rest upon his head and upon his people. But we were commanded not to make a blemish in the holy thing in order to eat them, for one who casts a blemish in the holy things by his own choice... also the prohibition of work and shearing in the holy things, for even the broken tablets are holy.

### **The total** of the burnt offering: the <term>Avodah</term> is the sacrifice, but the inner sacrifice is the man. Likewise, his soul is called after his death to the altar above, and Michael is the High Priest. The point is the secret that "in the image of God the man was made." Therefore, the warning comes to be careful in his life regarding damage to souls, not to put a man to death except after the interrogation and the examination thoroughly. Then he is judged by the hands of Heaven, in the secret of "He is the witness and He is the judge," for the Lord, blessed be He, is a true witness and a true judge. So must the <term>Sanhedrin</term> <gloss>high court</gloss> be; just as they are true judges, so must they be true witnesses. I mean to say that they must have the secret of the truth of the witnesses in complete clarity, which is the interrogation and the examination. Then their judgment is like the judgment of Heaven, and "Precious in the eyes of the Lord is the death [of His saints]."

### **And since** "Precious in the eyes of the Lord is the death," because Israel is holy by virtue of their souls, for after their death the souls adhere above, therefore the command comes, "You shall not cut yourselves, you shall not make a bald spot," etc., for "You are children to the Lord your God." This is not the case for the nations; the cutting and the baldness are from their customs, for it is appropriate since in their death they go to perdition and have no portion either in this world or in the World to Come. This is not so with us, the children of the Living God. When one is missing from this world, which is a temporary dwelling, on the contrary, we have a permanent dwelling above with our Father in Heaven. Therefore, it is forbidden to increase mourning and to perform these acts.

### **Let us return** to the matter that the man who works is himself the sacrifice, as it is written, "When a man offers from among you." Furthermore, there is a secret in this: for the sparks that are scattered even below in the man, that is, in the secret of the reincarnation of "Man and beast You save, O Lord." Therefore, even in the eating of ordinary food, the meat of desire, we were commanded in the slaughtering and in a great examination without any defect, for then it is <term>nevelah</term> <gloss>carrion</gloss>, and then it becomes carrion in Israel, for who knows what reincarnation is in it? "And you shall love your neighbor as yourself" implies for him a beautiful death, that is, slaughtering without defect. If the beast dies of itself, or if the power of impurity spreads and seizes it, but when one slaughters it properly, and there is in the beast—its sacrifice—and like a pure bird, a spark of holiness, then its soul departs in purity.

### **And one who eats** a limb from the living, it is as one who eats from the flesh of a person when there is a reincarnation of a soul there. This is the secret, "The soul shall not be eaten with the flesh." Likewise, the prohibition of forbidden foods, and the signs of the pure beast, wild animal, and bird, all point to the spark that is spread within them, if it is from the side of impurity or from the side of holiness. I have elaborated on this in the portion of <term>Shemini</term> <gloss>Eighth</gloss>, and Israel, when they conduct themselves in holiness, it is written of them, "And they shall make Me a sanctuary, and I shall dwell in their midst," for they themselves are the tabernacle, for the man is like three parts: the head corresponds to the Holy of Holies, the heart corresponds to the Holy Place, and then from the stomach onward corresponds to the Courtyard of the Sanctuary, as I elaborated in the portion of <term>Terumah</term> <gloss>Heave-offering</gloss>. When he eats foods that are from the side of holiness, then they are like a sacrifice offered upon the altar. Concerning this, the Sages of blessed memory said: "Now a man's table provides atonement," as I have elaborated in its place.

### **The matter** of the commandment of the appointed times and their sacrifices, I have written about the matters of each one in its special place. The commandment came to rejoice on the festivals and to ascend for the festival, and "Three times a year shall every male of yours appear." It does not say "go," but in the manner that he comes to see, so he comes to be seen. Therefore, if he wishes to be seen in the Temple, where the Glory dwells, he must be "turn from evil and do good" and be a faithful servant to his Creator. If not for this, it is forbidden to enter the hall of the wicked, and how could he wish to be seen before Him, blessed be He? He brings the burnt offering of appearance, and then he himself is a sacrifice by means of the sacrifice that he offers. And it said, "Three times a year he shall be seen"—Isaac, who lived, is a perfect burnt offering.

### On Shame Arising from Undeserved Praise.
## D I A L. XXVI.

> Spare your praise, for when you praise wrongly,
> If you condemn later, it will be a sign of fickleness.

*Sorrow.* I am accused of having praised an unworthy man.

<note>A large ornamental letter L initiates the response from Reason.</note>

*Reason.* You are accused of having praised an unworthy man. A thing that is evil often arises from a good root. For good and innocent people, just as they are themselves, think others to be the same. Hence, they are even more prone to praise than is reasonable. And although I admit that to praise an unworthy man is an evil, to disparage a deserving one is much worse.

*Sorrow.* I have praised an unworthy man.

*Reason.* If you did it knowingly, you are reprehensible; but if unknowingly, you are excusable. It is a lesser evil to be deceived than to deceive. For to be deceived is the experience of another, but to deceive is the specific crime of the deceiver.

*Sorrow.* Another's praise turns into my own infamy.

*Reason.* Rather, it is your own fault or ignorance. For there is no infamy in you from the praise of another, just as there is no praise in you from their infamy.

*Sorrow.* I grieve greatly that I have praised an unworthy man.

*Reason.* See to it, then, that you do not grieve over that very thing often. Beware lest you leap rashly into praising or blaming. For there is a lust for both, and (to speak precisely) it is a disease and a certain itch of a restless tongue, ignorant of stillness. Furthermore, they argue: just as natural bodies are subject to celestial bodies, so too do artificial bodies, such as images, acquire certain hidden virtues following the influence of celestial bodies. Therefore, artificial bodies like images acquire certain hidden virtues from celestial bodies to cause certain effects, and thus it is not illicit to use them and other things of this kind. Moreover, demons can transform bodies in many ways, as Augustine says in book three of *On the Trinity* <note>Augustine, *De Trinitate*, discusses the limits of demonic power.</note>, and this is evident in the bewitched. Therefore, it is licit to use their power to remove such afflictions.

One who is being purged must not hasten to consume many, low-quality foods, lest the <term>nature</term> <gloss>the body's innate regulating force</gloss> draw them in undigested. If any of this is required, it must be little by little, spaced out so that it is done gradually, and what enters the body must be well-digested.

<term>Phlebotomy</term> <gloss>bloodletting</gloss> is the specific evacuation for blood. As for evacuation specific to a <term>humor</term> <gloss>bodily fluid</gloss> that is excessive in quantity or corrupt in quality, it is something other than phlebotomy. Every evacuation that is excessive causes fainting in most cases. If its interruption leaves behind a habit of diarrhea, the illness <note>the underlying condition</note> usually returns, leading to a recurrence of that evacuation, as in the case of one who suffers from interrupted nosebleeds or nasal blockages, for if the habit returns, it takes it away. 

Know that the remaining material that needs to be purged is less receptive to extreme measures and reaching the point of exhausting one's strength. Often, nature digests that remainder on its own. As long as the humor is of the required type and the patient can tolerate it, do not fear excess; sometimes you may even need to purge until fainting. He whose strength is robust and whose quantity of poor humors is large should be purged little by little. Likewise, if the material is highly mature or strongly mixed with blood, it cannot be purged all at once. This is the case with sciatica, chronic joint pain, cancer, chronic scabies, and chronic boils. 

Know that diarrhea draws from above and expels from below, so it corresponds to the accustomed drawing. It also corresponds after the stabilization of materials. If the materials are from below, the opposite pulls them toward it and expels them from where they are, according to the action of attraction, and vice versa. The status of phlebotomy varies according to the locations from which the blood is taken, as you already know. The people least in need of evacuation are those with good digestion, and inhabitants of hot climates have little need for evacuation.

We say that it is recommended for one who wishes to purge to delay or separate their food. One should determine the amount to be experienced in a day, in one sitting, and make them different foods and different drinks. The stomach reacts to this situation by longing to push what is inside it either upward or downward. As for food that is not varied but is rather the same, the stomach becomes full of it, relaxes, and holds onto it very tightly, especially if it is small in quantity. As for the laxative, nothing is needed. 

Know that the need for vomiting, purgation, and the like does not arise for one who maintains a good <term>regimen</term> <gloss>lifestyle and diet management</gloss>. One who is in a good regimen needs what is milder than that. Exercise, massage, and cupping may suffice to eliminate it. If one’s body is filled with the most excellent of humors, meaning blood, then phlebotomy is what is needed for purification, not purgation. If necessity demands phlebotomy or evacuation, then, as Hippocrates says, evacuate first, and if that does not suffice, then phlebotomy. This is among the teachings of Hippocrates and the books that follow him, and it is the truth. 

This applies if the phlegmatic humors are mixed with blood. If the humors are equal, viscous, and cold, phlebotomy may increase their thickness and viscosity, so one must begin with purgation. In summary, if the humors are equal, prioritize phlebotomy; if they are not equal, prioritize evacuation until they are equal, then perform phlebotomy. Whoever prioritizes medicine before phlebotomy should have prioritized phlebotomy even a little bit. Whoever was recently phlebotomized and needs to purge, the medicine should be withheld from him. Often, the ingestion of medicine when phlebotomy was required results in fainting and agitation; if it is not calmed by sedatives, then phlebotomy should have been performed first. 

There is no evacuation needed for excess fullness unless the magnitude of the illness calls for it, and fullness is assessed according to quality and quantity. Often, one compensates through regimen rather than the phlebotomy that might be required at that time. Often, the need for evacuation arises, but an obstacle hinders it. The only solution is fasting, sleep, and correcting the temperamental imbalance in a way that addresses the fullness. Some evacuation is performed for the purpose of precaution, such as what is needed for those accustomed to gout, epilepsy, or other conditions at a known time, especially in the spring. Thus, it is necessary to take precautions before the time comes and perform the evacuation specific to it, whether it is phlebotomy or purgation. 

Sometimes, the use of external desiccants and drying medicines acts as an evacuation, such as what is done for those with dropsy. Sometimes, you are forced to use a medicine that corresponds to the evacuated humor in quality, such as <term>scammony</term> <gloss>a purgative plant resin</gloss> when you need to evacuate yellow bile. In that case, you must mix with it what differs in quality but agrees in purgation, such as <term>myrobalan</term> <gloss>a medicinal fruit</gloss>. If an imbalance arises afterward in patients with visceral tumors, their purgation weakens. If you are forced to do so, use for them substances such as spurge and safflower. As for the purgative, it is <term>cassia fistula</term> <gloss>purging cassia</gloss>. 

Hippocrates said that whoever has a stomach that easily responds to vomiting should first be purified by using vomiting in the summer or spring, at the right time, as this relieves the body of fatigue. Know that one who is accustomed to drinking milk or who is not accustomed to vomiting should avoid it when there is no need. One must proceed before purgation by softening the humor intended for evacuation and widening the passages at the time. Know that one who drinks milk or is not accustomed to vomiting should, before using strong medicine, engage in a regimen of reduction. Purgation that accompanies abdominal wasting is difficult and tiresome. 

A purgative medicine may sometimes act as a laxative if the stomach is strong, if it is drunk while extremely hungry, if the drinker is accustomed to milk, or because the medicine is heavier in substance than what descends quickly. The purgative may cause nausea due to weakness of the stomach, intensity of weight, the medicine causing discomfort, or the person having indigestion. Every purgative medicine, if it does not purge the undigested, excites the humor it is meant to purge and spreads it throughout the body, dominating the body and drawing other humors to it, thus increasing that humor in the body. Some humors are more responsive to vomiting in most cases, such as yellow bile, while others are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile. Some have a condition like milk and stars, where purgation is more appropriate. 

Those whose humor is descending, like those with intestinal slippage, find that the tightening of the intestines hinders the purgative medicine. What is composed of medicines that vary greatly in the time of purgation causes intestinal disturbance, and the first will purge before the second, or the first may even purge the second. Whoever is exposed to purgation and their body is not clean will inevitably suffer from colic and distress, and what is evacuated is evacuated with great difficulty. In general, medicine that evacuates waste products should not cause agitation. If it is taken and agitation occurs, it is either evacuating what is not waste, or the evacuated humor has changed to another humor, which indicates that the body is clean of the humor intended for evacuation.

Why, therefore, does God foreknow these uncertain future events? For if He deems that things are avoidable, and yet it is not possible for them not to occur, He is deceived, which is impious even to think, let alone to express. But if He discerns that things are to be future in such a way that He knows they can either happen or not happen, what kind of foreknowledge is this that grasps nothing certain, nothing stable? Or how does this differ from that ridiculous prophecy of Tiresias, who says, "Whatever I shall say, either it will be or it will not be"? 

How, also, would divine prudence differ from human opinion, if, like men, He judges uncertain things whose outcome is uncertain? But if, in that most certain fountain of all things, nothing uncertain—

<meta>continues from previous page: ...The third article. Whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.

It is proceeded thus, for the third. That more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition: because those things which are prior according to nature are posterior and less known according to us, but universals are prior according to the nature of our intellect. Furthermore, composites are prior according to us and simple things are posterior. But universals are prior in nature; therefore they are known later according to us. Furthermore, the philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the <term>Physics</term> <gloss>natural science</gloss> that the defined falls into our cognition prior to the parts of the definition and less universal [parts]: just as animal is a part of the definition of man, and universals are known later according to us. Furthermore, effects are known to us, and causes and principles are known later according to us. But universals are known later according to us. But it is argued <note>following the thought of the Philosopher in the first book of the Physics</note> to descend from singulars to <unclear>universals</unclear>. I answer that it must be said that in the cognition of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, that intellectual cognition in some way takes its beginning from sensitive [cognition]. And because the sense is of singulars, and the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars be prior to us than the cognition of universals. Second, it must be considered that our intellect proceeds from potency to act. And that which proceeds from potency to act arrives first at an incomplete act, which is the midpoint between potency and perfect act. The perfect act to which the intellect arrives is complete science, through which things are known distinctly and determinately; the incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is known in this way is known as in act and in a certain way in potency. As the Philosopher says in the first book of the <term>Physics</term>, what is manifest and certain to us first is more confused; afterwards we know [things] by distinguishing the principles and elements distinctly. It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained without having the proper knowledge of each of those things contained in it is to know something under a certain confusion. Thus, it can be known as a whole in which parts are contained in potency, and an integral whole; for each whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being known distinctly. However, to know distinctly that which is contained in the whole, or to have knowledge of a less common thing: just as to know animal indistinctly, and to know an animal in which it is rational or irrational, which is to know a man or a lion. Therefore, it occurs to our intellect first to know animal, and [then] to know man. And it falls under reason if I compare whichever to more or to less, just as sense goes from potency into act, so does the intellect; that order of <column-break/> cognition appears in the sense. For it is known more in the sense and with less [difficulty] at a distance through <unclear>that which is bodily</unclear>, and [the sense] perceives the animal; and it perceives the animal more, and it perceives the being, and prior to that the being and the <unclear>substance</unclear>. Or it is clear as a child from the beginning distinguishes [a person] and [not a person]; and in children from the beginning they call all men fathers. Afterwards, however, one terminates in each one, as the Philosopher says in the first book of the <term>Physics</term>: the manifest is known, and one who knows something indistinctly still knows it in potency, or [in a way that is] a fiction and a principle; thus he knows the <unclear>species</unclear> and can [eventually] know the particulars. And thus, by itself, indistinct cognition is the middle between potency and act. And that the cognition of singulars is prior according to us, and the cognition of the universal is posterior, both in sensitive cognition and intellectual cognition. If <unclear>we compare</unclear> sense and intellect, [then] the cognition of the more universal is prior to the cognition of the less universal. To the first, it must be said that by a twofold [measure] it can be considered. One is that which is considered by the intention of truth. And because the intention of truth and the true [are] the same, it has a relationship to many things; and when the abstraction of the intellect reaches this end, then in truth it is posterior. In the first book <term>De Anima</term> <gloss>On the Soul</gloss>, the universal is either nothing or it is posterior: but he <note>Plato</note> posited universals as substances, and in this consideration, it is true, more because particulars are not except by participation in the more universal existing substances, which are called ideas. In another way, it can be considered with respect to the nature itself of animality or humanity, as it is found in particulars. And thus there is a twofold order of nature. One is according to the way of generation and time, when those things which are imperfect and in potency are prior. And in this way, the more universal is prior in nature, which appears manifestly in the generation of man and animals; for the animal is generated before the man, as the Philosopher says in the book <term>De Generatione Animalium</term> <gloss>On the Generation of Animals</gloss>. Another is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as act is simply prior to potency in nature, and that which is perfect is prior to that which is imperfect; and by this way, the less universal is prior in nature, for the intention of nature does not rest in the generation of the animal, but intends to generate the man. To the second, it is said that the more universal is compared to the less universal as the whole, and by the whole it is made more universal, not only by [a small number] but by man and horse; as it can contain [what is] less universal in the future, not only the more universal but also others, like man not only in animal but in rational. Thus, therefore, animal considered in itself is prior in our cognition to man. If man is prior in our cognition, then animal is [prior] by its reason. To the third, it must be said that something can be known in two ways. In one way absolutely, as it is in itself, and thus nothing is known <unclear>entirely</unclear>. In another way, as it is a part of this whole, like stones; it is necessary that we know the whole before the parts. For we know the house in a certain confused way. Thus, therefore, it must be said that the defined, absolutely considered, is known prior to the definition. Otherwise, the defined would not be made known by it, but rather by the parts.</meta>

When the morning arrived, the judge entered before the Lion, accompanied by a group of the prominent members of his court, carrying the letter containing the excuses <note>or justifications</note> that Dimna had offered. The Lion took the letter and ordered them to withdraw from his presence.

He then sent for his mother and read the letter to her. It distressed her, and she said, "If I speak harshly to you, O King, do not be angry."

The Lion replied, "I will not be angry, so say whatever you wish."

She said, "I do not see that you recognize what harms you from what benefits you. I fear that Dimna, through the length of time you have spent deliberating his case, will stir up against you matters that you will be unable to sit through or stand before."

She then stood up and left while she was angry. The next day, the judge sent for Dimna and brought him out. He consulted with the scholars regarding him, but they did not say anything.

The judge then said to him, "Even if everyone present has remained silent and said nothing, their suspicions have gathered upon the fact that you are a criminal. There is no good for you in life after your guilt has been settled in their hearts. I see nothing better for you than to confess your crime. This will relieve your neck of the burden in the afterlife, and it may restore a good reputation to your situation for two reasons: the first is your ability to find ways out and to fabricate excuses <note>the text repeats this concept; original: "المعاذير"</note> that defend you, and the second is your confession of your guilt, choosing safety in the afterlife over safety in this world. For the scholars have said: Death in what is beautiful is better than life in what (124) is ugly."

Dimna replied to him, saying, "Judges do not pass judgment based on their suspicions, nor on the suspicions of the common people or the elite. You know that suspicion does not replace the truth in any way. Even if all of you suspect that I am the perpetrator of this crime, I know myself, and my knowledge of myself is a certainty in which there is no doubt. My situation has only become ugly in your eyes, if you are indeed so, because you have suspected that I have striven..."

A powerful enemy is in pursuit of us,

The jester came in, having ridden hard,
Having killed several Arabian horses on the road.
Gathered at the palace of the king of the people,
Why did such haste arrive, oh fool?
Due to his haste, he spoke incoherently,
A clamor and agitation in the palace of the king.
One put both hands to his cheeks,
The other, from suspicion and wailing,
From the howling, sedition, fear, and punishment,
Every heart had gone into a hundred kinds of fancies.
Everyone was making an omen based on conjecture,
As to what fire had fallen into the rug.
The king quickly sought and gave the way,
When he kissed the ground, he said, "What was it?"
Whoever asked about the state of that somber one,
He placed his hand on his lips, meaning, "Hush."
His fancy ignites this culture of his,

The condition of the sheikh, the judge, and the drinking of the Jews,
I asked of the wine-seller at dawn.

Hold your tongue, keep the veil, and drink the wine."

O cupbearer, spring is arriving and no money remains for wine,
Think of a plan, for the blood of the heart has come to a boil from sorrow.

Your love is a poverty, a youth, and a fresh spring,
Accept my excuse and cover my sin with the hem of your generosity.

How long will you speak like a candle?
The moth of desire has arrived, O lover, be silent.

O King of form and meaning, like whom,
No eye has ever seen and no ear has ever heard.

Remain as long as the blue robe accepts,
Your young fortune from the ancient sky wears clothing.

Last night a sharp-witted expert told me in secret,
"From you, nothing should be hidden from the wine-seller."

He said, "Take matters easily upon yourself, for by its nature,
The world treats those who strive hard with difficulty."

And then he gave a cup, from the radiance of which in the sky,
Venus began to dance and grasped her lute in her ear.

With a bloody heart, bring a smiling lip like the cup,
Do not raise a cry like a harp if you receive a wound.

Until you become an intimate, you will not hear the secret behind this veil,
The ear of the uninitiated is not a place for the message of <term>Soroush</term> <gloss>the messenger angel</gloss>.

When it was time for the King to turn the reins,
It is not fitting to find victory through theft.
The seeker began anew,
That Dara had prepared so much fat.
What one can count by comparison,
Those who are experts in identifying fat,
Iskandar said to him, "One sharp sword,
Can slice the fat of a hundred cows into pieces."
Such a noble response to the army,
Rose high from the noble monarch.
The news grew warmer every moment,
That a roaring dragon had arrived in Rome.
When Iskandar realized that this fierce cloud <note>referring to Dara's aggressive approach</note>,
Would brandish the lightning of the sword,
He sent word for the army from every land,
To hasten to the gate of the monarch.
From Egypt, Africa, Rome, and Russia,
A host was assembled like a bride.
When the boundless army became numerous,
He asked for the count of the renowned heroes.
The recruiter reported that three hundred thousand,
Gallant, singular horsemen had emerged.
When the army's affairs were fully arranged,
He formed an assembly outside, with wine and cups.
The alert minds of Rome sat together,
And with the seal of the King, they softened their hearts like wax.
The King spoke and delved into his affairs,
He discussed and entangled himself in his work.

At that moment, I realized and I came to my senses, but the time had passed. I became certain that his whole affair was a trick and a verse in a poem. Take heed from what has come to you; let your companions remember what has befallen you, so that you may always remember the misfortune that struck you. Expel from your memory your lost dirhams, and be patient for one who is tested and endures, and to whom the lesson becomes manifest so that he might learn."

I bade him farewell, while shame and sorrow overtook me, dragging the hem of loss and regret, and I intended to confront Abu Zayd with the news and speak to him openly.

When we saw that we were prepared to compose words that might be transmitted from us, it became incumbent upon us to make you the first to whom we presented what we possess, and whom we informed of what we have. For to cast toward you the ultimate conclusions we reached before we have established the principles with you would provide you with nothing more than a general, traditional matter. This is true if you hold a favorable opinion of us due to affection and friendship, not because we believe we deserve to have our word accepted. We are not satisfied for you with anything higher than this rank, nor are we content for you with this level itself, if it is not sufficient for salvation, let alone for achieving the highest stations.

We only wish to lead you upon the paths that we have already traveled, and to have you swim in the sea that we crossed first, until it brings you to where we arrived. Thus, you may witness what we witnessed, verify with your own insight all that we have verified, and have no need to tether your knowledge to what we have known. This requires a specific, significant amount of time, freedom from worldly distractions, and the application of one’s entire resolve to this art. If this determination is sincere in you, and your intention is sound for girding yourself for this pursuit, you will praise your journey in the morning, attain the blessing of your endeavor, and you will have pleased your Lord, and He will have pleased you. I will be for you where you desire in your hope, and toward which you strive with your ambition and your entire being. This is a great affliction, for which it is necessary to forbid anyone from delving into those sciences. For even if they are not related to matters of religion, yet because they are among the principles of their sciences, their evil and their misfortune spread <gloss>[70]</gloss> to him. **The Second Affliction:** This arises from a friend of Islam who is ignorant. He thought that religion ought to be supported by denying every science attributed to them, so he denied all their sciences and claimed they were ignorant in them. He even denied their statements regarding solar and lunar eclipses, claiming that what they said was contrary to the revealed law. When this reached the ears of someone who knew those things through definitive proof, he did not doubt their proof, but he believed that Islam is built upon ignorance and the denial of definitive proof. Thus, his love for philosophy increased, and his hatred for Islam intensified. It is a grave crime against religion for one to think that Islam is supported by denying these sciences. The revealed law does not address these sciences by way of negation or affirmation, nor do these sciences address religious matters. As for the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him:

3223. There are two lights by which man is illuminated: the light of the world and the light of heaven. The light of the world is from the sun; the light of heaven is from the Lord. The light of the world is for the natural or external man, and thus for those things that are within him. The things that are there, even if they do not appear to belong to that light, still are; for nothing can be grasped by the natural man except through such things as exist and appear in the solar world, and thus have some form only by the light and shadow there. All ideas of time and ideas of space, which make up so much of the natural man that he cannot think without them, also belong to the light of the world. However, the light of heaven is for the spiritual or internal man. The interior mind of man, where his intellectual ideas—which are called immaterial—reside, is in that light. Man does not know this, even though he calls his understanding "sight" and attributes light to it. The reason is that, as long as he is in worldly and corporeal things, he has perception only of such things as belong to the light of the world, and not of such things as belong to the light of heaven. The light of heaven is from the Lord alone; the entire heaven is in that light. This light—namely, the light of heaven—is immensely more perfect than the light of the world. Those things that form one ray in the light of the world form myriads in the light of heaven. In the light of heaven there is intelligence and wisdom. It is that light which flows into the light of the world—which is in the external or natural man—and causes him to perceive objects of things sensually. Unless that light flowed in, man would have no perception at all, for life is present in those things belonging to the light of the world from that source. Between these lights, or between those things that are in the light of heaven and in the light of the world, there exists a correspondence when the external or natural man makes one with the internal or spiritual man; that is, when the former serves the latter. What then exist in the light of the world are representative of those things that are in the light of heaven.

Those who are in the loves of self and of the world, and thus in the heat of the light of the world alone, are affected only by evils and falsities, and these are what extinguish the truths that are of the light of heaven. In this way, having taught up to the unmixed qualities of a Buddha, it is then taught that a Bodhisattva should not have an arrogant attachment even to the mind of enlightenment. Thus, the mind of enlightenment, along with its qualities, is taught.

The word "is" signifies that the waning <note>or diminution/decline</note> of constructed form is not the essence of the reality of phenomena. The Blessed One has stated that "suchness" <term>tathātā</term> <gloss>thusness/reality as it is</gloss> is impermanent. Regarding the statement "that which is the waning of suchness is not suchness," this should be applied through the distinction between that which is associated with defilement and that which is free from defilement. Since that which was previously associated with defilement later becomes free from defilement, it is therefore impermanent. In this way, regarding the suchness that is impermanent, one should apply the understanding that the waning of the suchness of form, the suchness of feeling, and so on, is not the suchness of the perfected nature.

Furthermore, regarding the statement, "Blessed One, what is called 'form' is categorized as non-dual," the term "non-dual" refers to the nature of phenomena, which is ultimate reality. The categorization of that ultimate reality is what is meant by such terms as "form," "feeling," and so on. What does this teach? It teaches that ultimate reality is singular and non-dual. However, through expressions such as "the form of the nature of phenomena," "the feeling of the nature of phenomena," "the perception of the nature of phenomena," "the compositional factors of the nature of phenomena," and "the consciousness of the nature of phenomena," the singular non-dual ultimate reality is explained as having been divided into many aspects.

Regarding the passage, "Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the venerable Subhūti," one may ask what this is connected to. It is connected to the fourfold explanation that the elder Subhūti provided immediately after explaining the result of non-conceptual mental engagement: "Blessed One, when a Bodhisattva, a great being, practices the Perfection of Wisdom and examines those phenomena in this way, at that time, they do not grasp, they do not take hold of, they do not abide in, and they do not become attached to form"—this is the first. "That which is the unborn nature of form is not form"—and so on—is the second. "That which is the waning of form is not form"—this is the third.

Even if one were to fill the worlds equal in number to the sands of the Ganges with the bodily relics of Tathāgatas, upholding the Perfection of Wisdom would still yield greater merit, along with its causes. What is called the "nature of conditioned phenomena" is the essence of wisdom characterized by conceptual thought. What is called the "nature of unconditioned phenomena" is that which is ineffable, the essence of the ultimate truth.

The three vehicles are explained extensively.
